summary.text: A marginal distribution gives the probabilities of some variables on their own, without reference to the values of the other variables.
From a joint table of two variables, you get one variable's marginal by summing over every value of the other, and the sums sit in the table's margins.
This contrasts with a conditional distribution, which gives probabilities that depend on the values of the other variables.

facts.label: Where the name comes from
facts.value: Sums along rows or columns are written in the table's margins

facts.label: How to get it
facts.value: Sum the joint distribution over all values of the other variable

facts.label: Versus conditional
facts.value: A conditional distribution depends on other variables' values

facts.label: Other variable
facts.value: Sum over X's values to get Y's marginal

facts.label: Traffic example
facts.value: Each light colour's hit chance is weighted by how often it occurs

items.prompt: A pedestrian's chance of being hit depends on the colour of the traffic light. You want the overall chance of being hit when the colour is unknown. What do you do?

options.label: Use the hit chance for the most common colour only
Add each colour's hit chance, weighted by how often that colour occurs
Take the plain average of the hit chances for the colours
Use the lowest of the colours' hit chances

items.explain: With the colour unknown, you sum the conditional chances over all colours, each weighted by the probability of that colour.

items.prompt: A table lists the chance of each combination of two results. How do you read off the chance of just one of those results, ignoring the other?

options.label: Pick the biggest cell in its row
Multiply all the cells in its row
Add up the cells along its row or column
Subtract the other result's total from 1

items.explain: Summing along rows or columns and writing the sums in the margins gives each variable's own probabilities.

items.prompt: A teacher has study time and test scores for a class. Which question looks at the scores with study time left out?

options.label: How are the scores spread across the whole class?
Among students who studied longest, how are scores spread?
Among students with top scores, how long did they study?
Do students who study longer tend to score higher?

items.explain: The marginal distribution of the scores is the distribution when study time is not taken into consideration. The other questions all depend on study time.

items.prompt: One friend says, "It rains on 30% of days." Another says, "It rains on 60% of the cloudy days." What makes the second statement different?

options.label: It sums over all weather conditions
It averages many days instead of one
It looks at one event on its own
It assumes another event has already occurred

items.explain: The first is a marginal probability of a single event. The second is conditional: it holds given that another event, cloud, has occurred.

items.prompt: You know X's marginal distribution is found by summing the joint distribution over all values of Y. How would you find Y's marginal?

options.label: Sum the joint distribution over the separate values of X
Divide X's marginal by the joint distribution
It cannot be found from the same joint distribution
Subtract X's marginal from 1

items.explain: The same works the other way round: summing over the values of X gives the marginal of Y.

items.prompt: In the traffic example, why is the overall chance of being hit found by adding the chances across the lights?

options.label: Being hit is always certain under at least one light
Each light colour is a separate way for a person to be hit
The chances under the lights must add up to 1 anyway
Only the green light matters for this sum

items.explain: A pedestrian can be hit if the light is red, or yellow, or green, so the separate chances are added, weighted by how often each colour occurs.
